Wisdom begins with relationships

Verse 8 names two teachers, a father and a mother. The mother’s teaching stands beside the father’s instruction. Verse 9 calls their words a wreath and a necklace. The first lesson that follows is about an invitation (verses 10–14). A gang says, “Come with us,” and promises one shared purse. The learner must choose between two sets of voices. Verses 18–19 say the violent men ambush themselves.
Learning requires a search

Verses 1–4 stack up conditions with the word “if.” Verse 5 answers with “then.” Verse 4 compares the search to mining for silver. Miners dig long and deep for what they value. Yet verse 6 says the LORD gives wisdom. The chapter holds both together. A person must search hard, and what he finds is still a gift.
Trust reaches a neighbor’s need

The chapter begins with trust in God (verses 5–6). It ends with neighbors (verses 27–30). Verse 27 speaks of good that is “due” to someone. The neighbor has a claim, and the learner has the means. Verse 28 names a common way to refuse: come again tomorrow. Delay can be a quiet form of saying no. Trust in God shows itself in prompt help.
A father repeats what he received

In verse 3 the teacher remembers being a child. His father taught him the words he now repeats (verse 4). Three generations stand in these verses. The teaching is handed on; the father did not invent it. Verse 23 puts the heart first as the source of life. Verses 24–27 then name the mouth, the eyes, and the feet. Guarding the inside comes before guarding the steps.
Water images distinguish shared commitment from wandering

Verses 15–18 speak of faithfulness through pictures of water. A cistern, a well, springs, and a fountain are named. In a dry land a household’s water was precious and guarded. Verse 16 pictures it spilled in the streets and wasted. The chapter does more than forbid. Verses 18–19 tell the man to delight in his own wife. The warning rests on a good thing worth keeping.
Different dangers share a need for attention

Verse 6 sends the learner to watch an insect. Wisdom can be gained by looking closely at the created world. Verse 7 notes that the ant has no chief or overseer. She works without being told. Verse 8 adds that she works at the right season. The chapter covers debts, laziness, troublemakers, and adultery. In each case a small lapse of attention leads to a large loss.
A warning unfolds as a scene

The warning comes as a scene the teacher watched (verses 6–7). The details matter. Verse 8 says the youth walked toward her corner, so he chose the street. Verse 9 marks the time as twilight turning to dark. Her speech uses religion (verse 14) and promises no one will know (verses 19–20). Verses 22–23 compare him to an ox, a deer, and a bird. A story lets the learner see the steps before the fall.
Wisdom speaks beyond the household

Wisdom speaks in the open, at the gates where everyone passes (verse 3). The woman of chapter 7 worked at dusk in a side street. In verse 22 Wisdom gives her age. She was with the LORD before any of his works. Verses 27–30 place her beside him at creation. So living wisely fits the way the world was made. Verses 30–31 add that she rejoiced in the world and in people.
Similar invitations conceal different endings

Verse 4 and verse 16 are the same invitation, word for word. Two hosts call the same people in the same way. The learner must look past the words to what each has ready. Wisdom built a house and cooked a meal (verses 1–2). Folly offers stolen water and secret bread (verse 17). Verse 6 ends in life, and verse 18 ends among the dead. This chapter closes the book’s long opening lessons.
Short sayings require a supplied situation

From this chapter the sayings stand alone, two lines each. The second line often contrasts with the first. No story surrounds them. The reader must supply the situation where each one fits. Verse 19 says more talk gives more room for wrong. Restraint of the lips is called wisdom. Many sayings in this chapter concern speech (verses 11, 13, 18, 20–21, 31–32).
A proverb makes trade a moral decision

Verse 1 calls a rigged scale an “abomination.” Other texts use that strong word for idols. Leviticus 19:35–36 and Deuteronomy 25:13–16 give the law behind it. A buyer could not easily test a seller’s weights. The poor, who bought in small amounts, were hurt most. An ancient trade weight shows the kind of tool the saying has in view. Verse 26 applies the same concern to those who hoard grain.
Words can wound or heal

Verse 18 treats words as a weapon or a medicine. The harmful speaker is called rash. He may not mean harm; he simply does not think first. The wound is as real as a sword cut. The wise tongue is said to heal. Verse 25 gives an example: one good word lifts a heavy heart. Verse 19 adds that true words last and lies do not.
Delay gives desire a bodily cost

Verse 12 gives no command. It describes what waiting does to a person. A hope delayed again and again makes the heart sick. A longing fulfilled is called a tree of life. Verse 19 repeats that a desire met is sweet. The saying helps a reader understand another person’s weariness. Verse 23 adds that poverty can come from injustice, not from laziness.
Appearance can conceal grief

This chapter keeps setting how things seem against how they are. Verse 12 says a road can look right and lead to death. Verse 13 applies that to a face. A person may laugh while the heart is in pain. Verse 10 says each heart knows its own bitterness. So the reader should be slow to judge by appearances. Verse 31 ties the treatment of the poor to respect for God.
Speech changes the direction of conflict

Verse 1 says the direction of a quarrel depends on the reply. A gentle answer is not a weak one. It “turns away” wrath, which is an active result. A harsh word feeds the fire. Verse 18 says a patient person calms a dispute. Verse 28 says the righteous think before they answer. Verse 23 praises the word that comes at the right moment.
Planning does not give complete control

Verse 9 keeps two truths together. People plan their course, and the saying does not discourage that. The LORD directs the actual steps. Verses 1 and 33 make the same point at the chapter’s two ends. Outcomes are not fully in human hands. That leads to the warning about pride in verse 18. Verse 32 values rule over oneself above victory in war.
Peace changes the value of abundance

Verse 1 is a “better than” saying. It compares a dry scrap with a table full of meat. The peace at the table decides which is better. A feast with quarreling is the poorer meal. Sayings in 15:16–17 make the same judgment. Verse 14 adds advice on how to keep that peace. A quarrel starts like a leak in a dam, so stop it early.
A hearing must precede judgment

Verse 13 states a basic rule of fairness and of courtesy. A person must hear before he answers. Verse 17 applies the rule to disputes. The first speaker sounds right until the other side is heard. Verse 2 describes the opposite habit. The fool wants to talk and not to understand. Verse 15 says the ear of the wise seeks knowledge.
Wealth can distort friendship

Verse 4 reports a fact about money and friendship. It does not approve of it. Verses 6–7 add that even a poor man’s brothers avoid him. The chapter then judges what it has observed. Verse 17 says kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD. Verses 1 and 22 say an honest poor person is better than a liar. The saying trains the reader to notice how wealth bends loyalty.
Fair judgment begins in ordinary tools

Verse 10 speaks of “differing weights.” A cheating trader kept two sets, one heavy and one light. He bought with one and sold with the other. Deuteronomy 25:13–14 forbids keeping both in the bag. Verse 23 repeats the saying in this same chapter. Verse 14 shows the buyer lying too. An ancient trade weight shows the kind of tool the saying has in view.
Ritual cannot substitute for justice

Verse 3 ranks right conduct above offerings. The prophets say the same in 1 Samuel 15:22 and Hosea 6:6. Micah 6:6–8 asks the question at length. The wisdom teachers and the prophets agree here. Verse 27 goes further about worship offered with evil intent. Verse 13 gives one concrete test. A person who ignores the poor will find his own cry ignored.
A shared maker limits social divisions

Verse 2 does not deny the gap between rich and poor. Verse 7 admits that the rich rule and lenders hold power. Verse 2 says where the two “meet.” One Maker formed them both. Neither stands higher before him. Verses 22–23 draw out a result for the courts. The LORD himself argues the case of the poor.
Hospitality may carry a hidden price

Verses 6–8 describe a host who resents what his guest eats. He says, “Eat and drink,” and his heart is not in it (verse 7). He counts each bite. The meal becomes a debt the guest did not agree to. Verses 1–3 gave a similar warning about a ruler’s table. Both passages treat a dinner as a place of hidden bargaining. Verses 10–11 name God as the defender of orphans’ land.
Knowing creates a duty to act

Verse 11 gives a duty: rescue people being taken to their death. Verse 12 closes the usual excuse. Someone may say, “We didn’t know this.” God weighs hearts and knows whether that is true. He can tell real ignorance from a choice not to look. Knowing creates a duty to act. Verses 30–34 show the teacher learning by looking at a ruined field.
Collected sayings connect wisdom with government

Verse 1 says Hezekiah’s men copied this collection. That was long after Solomon’s time (2 Kings 18:1). Royal scribes cared for these sayings. Verse 2 then describes a king’s proper work. God’s world holds more than its surface shows. A ruler honors his office by finding out the truth of a matter. Verse 8 applies that: do not hurry into court.
Paired sayings require judgment

Verses 4 and 5 contradict each other on purpose. One says not to answer a fool, and the next says to answer him. Each gives a good reason. Silence avoids sinking to his level. A reply keeps him from thinking he has won. The reader must judge which fits the moment. Verses 7 and 9 warn that a proverb in the wrong mouth does harm.
Care requires knowledge of actual conditions

The chapter ends with a short poem about herding (verses 23–27). Verse 23 says to “know well” the condition of the animals. A herder must look at the actual flock and not assume. Verse 24 gives the reason: wealth and even a crown do not last. A living flock renews itself if someone cares for it. Verse 27 includes the servant girls in what it provides. The friendship sayings in verses 6, 9, and 17 also ask for close attention.
Profit can reveal a damaged relationship

Exodus 22:25 and Leviticus 25:36 forbid taking interest from a poor neighbor. Verse 8 describes someone who grows rich that way. The saying claims the money will not stay with him. It ends in the hands of a person who pities the poor. Proverbs states such things as the way God’s world tends to go. They are not promises for every single case. Verse 11 adds that a poor person with insight sees through the rich.
Justice requires learning the poor person’s case

Verse 7 says the righteous “care about” the rights of the poor. Caring here includes learning the facts of their case. That takes time and effort. The wicked, the verse says, have no interest in such knowledge. Not caring becomes a kind of ignorance. Verse 14 applies the point to kings who judge. Verse 13 repeats that the LORD gives light to both poor and powerful.
A prayer questions both extremes of wealth

Verses 7–9 are the only prayer in the book of Proverbs. Agur sees danger at both ends of wealth. Verse 9 explains each one. A full person may ask, “Who is the LORD?” A hungry person may steal and dishonor God’s name. So verse 8 asks for the food that is needed. Jesus teaches a similar request for daily bread in Matthew 6:11.
A mother’s instruction reaches public judgment

The king’s teacher here is his mother, as in 1:8. Verse 8 gives her view of what power is for. A king should open his mouth for the “mute.” These are people who have no voice in court. Verse 9 adds fair judgment for the poor and needy. The poem in verses 10–31 then shows wisdom at work in a household. The book began with Wisdom as a woman and ends with a wise woman.
